summary: Waseem Alshikh, CTO and Co-founder of Writer, delivers a talk at the AI Engineer Summit 2025 addressing whether domain-specific LLMs remain necessary as general-purpose models improve. Writer, founded in 2020, has published approximately 16 models across two categories: general models (Palmyra X, P3, P4, with Palmyra 5 upcoming) and domain-specific models (Creative, Financial Services, Medical). In early 2024, with general models achieving 80-90% accuracy on benchmarks, Writer questioned whether to continue building domain-specific models or pivot entirely toward reasoning/thinking models. To answer this, they created FAIL, a benchmark evaluating models on real-world financial scenarios with two main categories. Query failure includes misspelled queries, incomplete queries, and out-of-domain queries. Context failure includes missing context, OCR errors (from document-to-text conversion), and irrelevant context (wrong document uploaded). The benchmark, data, and leaderboard are open-sourced on GitHub and Hugging Face. The evaluation measured both answer correctness and context grounding. Key findings reveal that thinking models rarely refuse to answer but fail significantly at following provided context, leading to higher hallucination rates. Larger thinking models (o1, O3) showed 50-60% worse grounding performance, while smaller models outperformed them on grounding. The best model achieved only ~81% combined robustness and grounding, meaning approximately 1 in 5 requests is completely wrong. Waseem concludes that domain-specific models remain necessary today, and reliable systems require a full-stack approach including RAG, grounding, and guardrails, not just model improvements alone.

sections.title: Introduction and Writer History
sections.summary: Waseem introduces himself as Co-founder and CTO of Writer, founded in 2020. Writer has been building Transformer-based models since the early days, now with ~16 published models and ~20 more in development across two categories: general models (Palmyra X, P3, P4, Palmyra 5 upcoming) and domain-specific models (Creative, Financial Services, Medical).

sections.title: The Core Question: General vs Domain-Specific Models
sections.summary: In early 2024, general models reached 80-90% accuracy on benchmarks, prompting Writer to question whether building domain-specific models remains worthwhile. They considered pivoting toward reasoning/thinking models instead. To answer this, they needed data and created a financial benchmark called FAIL.

sections.title: FAIL Benchmark Design: Query and Context Failures
sections.summary: FAIL evaluates models on real-world financial scenarios with two categories. Query failure includes misspelled queries, incomplete queries, and out-of-domain queries. Context failure includes missing context, OCR errors from document conversion, and irrelevant context from wrong documents. The benchmark, data, and leaderboard are open-sourced on GitHub and Hugging Face. Evaluation metrics focus on answer correctness and context grounding.

sections.title: Evaluation Results: Thinking Models Fail at Grounding
sections.summary: Results show thinking models rarely refuse to answer but fail badly at context grounding, producing higher hallucination. Larger thinking models (o1, O3) show 50-60% worse grounding. Smaller models outperform on grounding. The gap between robustness and grounding is significant, suggesting these models may be doing Chain of Thought rather than genuine thinking in domain-specific tasks.

sections.title: Conclusion: Full-Stack Approach and Domain-Specific Models Still Needed
sections.summary: Even the best model achieves only ~81% combined robustness and grounding, meaning 1 in 5 requests is completely wrong. Waseem concludes that domain-specific models remain necessary today and that reliable systems require a full-stack approach including RAG, grounding, and guardrails. The answer to whether to keep building domain-specific models is yes.
